notes.text: He assures Moses it should now be done, ver. 7-9.
He gives him a commission to act in it as his ambassador both to Pharaoh, ver. 10, and to Israel, ver. 16.
He answers the objection Moses made of his own unworthiness, ver. 11, 12.
He gives him full instructions what to say, both to Pharaoh and to Israel, ver. 13-18.

He tells him before-hand what the issue would be, ver. 14-22.

1. Now Moses - The years of Moses's life are remarkably divided into three forties; the first forty he spent as a prince in Pharaoh's court, the second a shepherd in Midian, the third a king in Jeshurun. He had now finished his second forty when he received his commission to bring Israel out of Egypt. Sometimes it is long before God calls his servants out to that work which of old he designed them for. Moses was born to be Israel's deliverer, and yet not a word is said of it to him till he is eighty years of age. Even to Horeb - Horeb and Sinai were two tops of the same mountain.

2. And the angel of the Lord appeared to him - It was an extraordinary manifestation of the divine glory; what was visible was produced by the ministry of an angel, but he heard God in it speaking to him. In a flame of fire - To shew that God was about to bring terror and destruction to his enemies, light and heat to his people, and to display his glory before all. And the bush burned, and yet was not consumed - An emblem of the church now in bondage in Egypt, burning in the brick-kilns, yet not consumed; cast down, but not destroyed.

3. I will turn aside and see - He speaks as one inquisitive, and bold in his inquiry; whatever it was, he would if possible know the meaning of it.

4. When the Lord saw that he turned aside to see it, God called to him - If he had carelessly neglected it, it is likely God had departed and said nothing to him. God called and said, Moses, Moses - This which he heard could not but surprise him much more than what he saw. Divine calls are then effectual, when the spirit of God makes them particular, and calls us as by name. The Word calls, Ho, every one; the Spirit, by the application of that, calls, Ho, such a one; I know thee by name. Here am I - Not only to hear what is said, but to do what I am bidden.

5. Put off thy shoes from off thy feet - The putting off the shoe was then what the putting off the hat is now, a token of respect and submission. The ground is holy ground, made so by this special manifestation of the divine presence. We ought to approach to God with a solemn pause and preparation; and to express our inward reverence, by a grave and reverent behaviour in the worship of God, carefully avoiding every thing that looks light, or rude.

I am the God of thy father — He lets him know it is God that speaks to him, to engage his reverence, faith and obedience. Thy father, thy pious father Amram, and the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, thy ancestors. Engaged to them by solemn covenant, which I am now come to perform. And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look upon God - The more we see of God, the more cause we shall see to worship him with reverence and godly fear. And even the manifestations of God's grace should increase our humble reverence of him.

I am come down to deliver them — When God doth something very extraordinary, he is said to come down to do it, as Isaiah lxiv, 1. This deliverance was typical of our redemption by Christ, and in that the eternal Word did indeed come down from heaven to deliver us. A large land - So it was, according to its true and ancient bounds, as they are described, Gen. xv, 18, and not according to those narrow limits, to which they were afterwards confined for their unbelief and impiety. A land flowing with milk and honey - A proverbial expression, abounding with the choicest fruits, both for necessity and delight.

I will send thee — And the same hand that now fetched a shepherd out of a desert to be the planter of the Jewish church, afterwards fetched fishermen from their ships to be the planters of the Christian church, that the excellency of the power might be of God.

Who am I? — He thinks himself unworthy of the honour and unable for the work. He thinks he wants courage, and therefore cannot go to Pharaoh: he thinks he wants conduct, and therefore cannot bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt; they are unarmed, undisciplined, quite dispirited, utterly unable to help themselves, Moses was incomparably the fittest of any man living for this work, eminent for learning, wisdom, experience, valour, faith, holiness, and yet Who am I? The more fit any person is for service, commonly the less opinion he has of himself.

Certainly I will be with thee — Those that are weak in themselves, yet may do wonders being strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. God's presence puts wisdom and strength into the weak and foolish, and is enough to answer all objections.

When they shall say to me, What is his name? What shall I say unto them? — What name shall I use, whereby thou mayest be distinguished from false gods, and thy people may be encouraged to expect deliverance from thee?

And God said — Two names God would now be known by.

1. A name that speaks what he is in himself, I am that I am - This explains his name Jehovah, and signifies, 1st, That he is self- existent; he has his being of himself, and has no dependence upon any other. And being self-existent he cannot but be self-sufficient, and therefore all-sufficient, and the inexhaustible fountain of being and bliss. 2ndly, That he is eternal and unchangeable, always the same, yesterday today, and forever: he will be what he will be, and what he is. 3rdly. That he is faithful and true to all his promises, unchangeable in his word as well as in his nature, and not a man that he should lie. Let Israel know this, I am hath sent me unto you.

2. A name that speaks what he is to his people. Lest that name I am should puzzle them, he is farther directed to make use of another name of God, more familiar.

The Lord God of our fathers hath sent me unto you — Thus God made himself known, that he might revive among them the religion of their fathers, which was much decayed, and almost lost. And that he might raise their expectations of the speedy performance of the promises made unto their fathers: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are particularly named, because with Abraham the covenant was first made, and with Isaac and Jacob oft expressly renewed, and these three were distinguished from their brethren, and chosen to be the trustees of the covenant. This God will have to be his name forever, and it has been, is, and will be his name, by which his worshippers know him, and distinguish him from all false gods.

glossa.text:
*And there appeared to him.* ((ISID.)) *Allegorically.* There was a flame in the bramble, and it was not burnt up. The bramble, the thorns of the sins of the Jews: the flame in the bramble, the word of God, that is, the law given to that people. But the flame does not burn up the bramble, because the law that was given does not consume their sins. Others understand by the flaming bramble the Church, which is set aflame by persecutions, and which, when the Lord speaks to her, is not burnt up. That the Lord appeared to Moses in the bramble shows that he appears to the faithful in the Church, and nowhere else. The Hebrews say that God appeared to Moses in a bramble for this reason, that the Jews might not be able to carve themselves an idol out of it. For God always cuts away the occasion of idolatry.

((GREG. lib. XXII Moral., cap. 20.)) Moses, mingled with the Egyptians, was as it were awake to the world, and therefore did not hear the voice of the Lord: but when the Egyptian had been slain, after he fled into the desert, while he dwelt there forty years, he fell asleep to earthly tumults, and therefore he perceived the divine voice. For when the mind is lulled from outward things, the word of God penetrates more truly. For the throng of earthly thoughts, clamouring about it, closes the ear of the heart. For a man does not perfectly suffice for both things when he is divided, because if he opens his hearing outwardly, he grows deaf within.

*And the Lord seeing,* etc. ((GREG., praef. in Moral., c. 2.)) The angel who is described as having appeared to Moses is recorded now as the Lord, now as an angel: an angel, because by speaking outwardly he serves; the Lord, because presiding inwardly he bestows the efficacy of speaking. For when he who speaks is governed from within, he is recorded both as an angel through his service, and as the Lord through his inspiration.

*He called him out of the midst,* etc. ((GREG. lib. XXVIII Moral., c. 5.)) Often God speaks through angels to earthly and to heavenly substances at once: as here, when he joined the fire and the bramble, and united one thing above and another below. Which is then only done, when something great is signified by the conjunction. For in addressing Moses through the kindled bramble, he showed that he would become a teacher of the people, one who should both receive the flame of the law and not shun the thorn of sin: so that from that people should come forth one who by the fire of the Godhead should take the sins of our flesh as it were the thorn of the bramble, and should preserve the substance of his humanity unconsumed in that very flame of the Godhead.

*Loose thy shoe,* etc. ((THEOD.)) For two reasons he bids him loose his shoes: first, that he may render him more and more religious and reverent, so that he may receive his commands with trembling; then also he is taught by what reason the priests should minister in the tabernacle of God: for they discharged the priestly office with bare feet.

 ((ISID.)) Because, namely, no one can worthily stand, or see God, unless he lay aside all things earthly and mortal. Otherwise, it was the custom of the ancients that if a bridegroom repudiated his bride, in sign of the repudiation he should be unshod. Therefore Moses is bidden to be unshod, and not to approach shod, as a bridegroom, to the Church, which is signified in the bramble; for this is to be reserved for Christ, who is the true bridegroom. Of whom John says: « Whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to loose ((Joan. I)).

*I am the God,* etc. ((HILAR. lib. IV de Trinitate.)) We must not speak of God otherwise than as he himself has spoken of himself to our understanding. It is an angel of God who appeared in the fire out of the bramble: and out of the bramble in the fire God speaks; thou hast the dispensation in the angel, because in the angel it is an office, not a nature; thou hast God in the name of nature, because the angel of God is God.

*I have seen the affliction,* etc. ((GREG., Moral. )) For minds scattered abroad it is hard for each to return to himself: because evil ways hold those once taken so delightfully, in proportion as what has pleased is not lawful. Because, when the gift of discipline does not stand in the way, no penalty of retribution is foreseen to terrify. But with the eyes of the heart closed the soul is cast headlong, and penetrates temporal evils the more securely, the more harshly it despairs of eternal goods. But this wickedness of the reprobate separates the life of the elect, as grains from chaff, and while it afflicts, it sets free: because while it presses violently, it compels men to hasten to things above; which in the Israelite people, when Moses called and Pharaoh raged, is signified. For Moses was sent to call, when Pharaoh pressed with hard works, so that the one by calling might draw, the other by raging might drive, that the people, basely fixed in servitude, might be moved either by being called or by being driven; this is done daily while, the heavenly rewards being preached, the reprobate are permitted to rage against the elect: so that those whom Egypt, that is, the present life, has oppressed by flattering, it may help by pressing; so that while God calls, torment may drive.

*And I will bring out of the land,* etc. ((GREG., homil. 32.)) To a rude people something had to be promised concerning the present life, that it might be able to be more sturdily strengthened in the future. For if it did not receive small things, it would not believe great ones. God therefore by bestowing earthly things persuades to heavenly things also, so that receiving what it saw, it might hope for what it did not see.

*Into a good and spacious land, in a land which flows with milk,* etc. ((Ibid.)) Present prosperity is sometimes given that it may call to a better life, sometimes that it may more fully condemn for ever. Hence to the Israelites the land of Chanaan is promised, that they may at some time be called to hope for things eternal: because a rude people would not believe promises, unless it received something near at hand from the promiser. Not therefore by hope alone is it drawn to things, but sometimes by things to hope. Whence Psalm CIV: *And he gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of the peoples, that they might keep his justifications and seek after the law.*

*He who is hath sent me to you,* etc. Moses is sent to punish Pharaoh and at last to slay him: the law was sent to destroy the devil.

Jerome, writing to Marcella concerning the ten names of God, puts in the sixth place the name *ehieh* ( אהיה ), which is read in Exodus: *He who is hath sent me to you.* For God alone, who has no beginning, holds the name of true essence: which was spoken by an angel to Moses when he asked his name, because in comparison with him who truly is, because he is unchangeable, the things that are changeable are as though they were not; for what is said to have been, is not: and what is said will be, is not yet. But God only is, who knows not to have been, or to be about to be. And the Father alone with the Son and the Holy Spirit truly is. Compared with whose essence, our being is not; whence also we say: God lives, because the divine essence lives by a life which death does not possess.

notes.text: Glory — Glory in the God whom you serve, as the only true God.
Seek — The Lord in his strength, in his sanctuary, or before the ark, which is called God's strength. Face - His gracious presence.
Judgments — The punishments which he brought upon Egypt by his mere word.
Of Jacob — The only branch of Abraham's seed to whom the following blessings belong.

glossa.text:
*Alleluia.* ((CASS.)) Here for the first time *alleluia,* nor was it set down before this by anyone; and no tongue has presumed to change it. *Alleluia,* praise ye. *Ia* is the name of the invisible God, which belongs to him alone. Through twenty psalms, which have this title, the great works of God are told, and great is the exultation in them. ((CASS.)) Here the prophet commends the good among that people of Israel, who together with other believers are the true seed of Abraham, the children of the promise.

*Give glory to the Lord.* ((AUG.)) The first psalm to which alleluia is prefixed, etc., *as far as* he subjoins what temporal things the mercy of God gave them.
*All things:* ((CASS.)) all things; there is nothing that shame should keep silent. Or, all the things which they shall tell are wonderful, for no one can relate them all.

*Be ye praised in the name,* that is, rejoice that you are called Christians from Christ.

((AUG.)) Be ye praised: he does not forbid being praised, if they are good; if they are not, then not save in the Lord, who makes men good. Be ye praised in the name. Which elsewhere is, *In the Lord shall my soul be praised:* what he adds there, *let the meek hear and rejoice:* here too in a manner, *let the heart rejoice,* as if he should say,

*The face,* etc. ((ID.)) That is, the presence, etc., *as far as* the wicked man can fear the presence which the good man loves. ((HIER.)) From the martyr Hippolytus, etc., *as far as* there about to take his Church from among the Gentiles.

*Remember, and the rest.* ((AUG.)) Seek him, etc., *as far as* if it is a great thing to seek what God is, at least behold the things which he has made. *The wonders,* etc. ((ID.)) Little by little he ascends from visible wonders to judgments: thence to the everlasting testament, where there is both precept and promise.

notes.text: Having spoken of faith and its fruit, ver. 3, &c., he comes now to love. The ninth, tenth, and eleventh verses refer to chapter the seventh; the twelfth verse to chapter the eighth; the thirteenth verse, of communicating to the saints, whether Jews or gentiles, to chapter the ninth, &c. Part of the sixteenth verse is repeated from chap. xi, 25. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good — Both inwardly and outwardly, whatever ill-will or danger may follow.
In honour preferring one another — Which you will do, if you habitually consider what is good in others, and what is evil in yourselves.
Whatsoever ye do, do it with your might. In every business diligently and fervently serving the Lord — Doing all to God, not to man.

Rejoicing in hope — Of perfect holiness and everlasting happiness. Hitherto of faith and love; now of hope also, see the fifth and eighth chapters; afterwards of duties toward others; saints, ver. 13 persecutors, ver. 14 friends, strangers, enemies, ver. 15, &c.

Communicate to the necessities of the saints — Relieve all Christians that are in want. It is remarkable, that the apostle, treating expressly of the duties flowing from the communion of saints, yet never says one word about the dead. Pursue hospitality - Not only embracing those that offer, but seeking opportunities to exercise it.
Curse not — No, not in your heart.
Rejoice — The direct opposite to weeping is laughter; but this does not so well suit a Christian.
Mind not high things — Desire not riches, honour, or the company of the great.
Provide — Think beforehand; contrive to give as little offense as may be to any.

Dearly beloved — So he softens the rugged spirit. Revenge not yourselves, but leave that to God. Perhaps it might more properly be rendered, leave room for wrath; that is, the wrath of God, to whom vengeance properly belongs. Deut. xxxii, 35

Feed him — With your own hand: if it be needful, even put bread into his mouth. Heap coals of fire upon his head - That part which is most sensible. "So artists melt the sullen ore of lead, By heaping coals of fire upon its head; In the kind warmth the metal learns to glow, And pure from dross the silver runs below." Prov. xxv, 21, &c.
And if you see no present fruit, yet persevere. Be not overcome with evil — As all are who avenge themselves. But overcome evil with good. Conquer your enemies by kindness and patience.

glossa.text:
*Not slothful.* Cursed is he that does the work of God negligently; the slothful man is without hope in the divine converse. And therefore, that the cold of sloth may be driven off, *Be ye fervent,* etc.

*Fervent in spirit. ((THEOD.))* He called grace the Spirit, etc., *as far as* for this he said. *Instant in prayer.* That is, doing this assiduously.

*Serving the Lord,* etc. As if he should say: Although I have said that ye should be fervent in spirit, yet do not thrust in the words of God everywhere and unseasonably, but be fervent with the opportunity of the time, so that ye may speak the words of faith in fit places, to fit persons, and at a fit time. *Fervent.* The Spirit is fire, with which charity is fervent, whence the Lord says: *I am come to send fire on the earth, and what will I, but that it burn? ((Luc. XII.))*
*Rejoicing in hope.* Being certain of things to come they rejoice, and therefore are patient in tribulation.

*Consenting.* Which is not done with the mouth only, because then is there true humility, if it is not in the tongue alone, lest, presuming upon themselves, they should not suffer with others, but reproach them.

*Give place.* He does not command that the saints should be unwilling to be avenged by God, which the saints cry out for in the Apocalypse, not indeed for the glutting of hatred, but because it is written: *The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge.* But he commands that they, not avenging themselves, give place to the wrath of God, who says: *Revenge to me, and I will repay.* If therefore a good man wills that God punish his enemy, this is not to render evil for evil. Since therefore both the just man and the evil man wish to be avenged by God on their enemies, wherein are they distinguished? The good man desires rather that his enemy be corrected than punished, and when God punishes he is not delighted at his enemy's pain, but that pleases him which pleases the Lord also, because he loves him, and it is God whom he follows in this: *Who raineth upon the just and the unjust ((Prov. XXV))*; and yet even in this world he more sharply reproves the obstinate and at the end will damn them, to whom accordingly vengeance is to be reserved. He gives place to the wrath of his adversary who permits his adversary to do what he will.

*But if he hunger.* Note the strangeness of the conjunction *but.* For it is to be carried on as though neither conjunction had been interposed. Or it can also be read thus, so that neither conjunction is superfluous, as if he should say, not only do ye not defend yourselves, but if, etc.

notes.text: From that time Jesus began to tell his disciples, that he must suffer many things — Perhaps this expression, began, always implied his entering on a set and solemn discourse. Hitherto he had mainly taught them only one point, That he was the Christ. From this time he taught them another, That Christ must through sufferings and death enter into his glory. From the elders - The most honourable and experienced men; the chief priests - Accounted the most religious; and the scribes - The most learned body of men in the nation. Would not one have expected, that these should have been the very first to receive him? But not many wise, not many noble were called. favour thyself - The advice of the world, the flesh, and the devil, to every one of our Lord's followers. Mark viii, 31; Luke ix, 22.

Get thee behind me — Out of my sight. It is not improbable, Peter might step before him, to stop him. Satan - Our Lord is not recorded to have given so sharp a reproof to any other of his apostles on any occasion. He saw it was needful for the pride of Peter's heart, puffed up with the commendation lately given him. Perhaps the term Satan may not barely mean, Thou art my enemy, while thou fanciest thyself most my friend; but also, Thou art acting the very part of Satan, both by endeavouring to hinder the redemption of mankind, and by giving me the most deadly advice that can ever spring from the pit of hell. Thou savourest not - Dost not relish or desire. We may learn from hence,

1. That whosoever says to us in such a case, favour thyself, is acting the part of the devil:

2. That the proper answer to such an adviser is, Get thee behind me:

3. That otherwise he will be an offense to us, an occasion of our stumbling, if not falling:

4. That this advice always proceeds from the not relishing the things of God, but the things of men. Yea, so far is this advice, favour thyself, from being fit for a Christian either to give or take, that if any man will come after Christ, his very first step is to deny, or renounce himself: in the room of his own will, to substitute the will of God, as his one principle of action.

If any man be willing to come after me — None is forced; but if any will be a Christian, it must be on these terms, Let him deny himself, and take up his cross - A rule that can never be too much observed: let him in all things deny his own will, however pleasing, and do the will of God, however painful. Should we not consider all crosses, all things grievous to flesh and blood, as what they really are, as opportunities of embracing God's will at the expense of our own? And consequently as so many steps by which we may advance toward perfection? We should make a swift progress in the spiritual life, if we were faithful in this practice. Crosses are so frequent, that whoever makes advantage of them, will soon be a great gainer. Great crosses are occasions of great improvement: and the little ones, which come daily, and even hourly, make up in number what they want in weight. We may in these daily and hourly crosses make effectual oblations of our will to God; which oblations, so frequently repeated, will soon amount to a great sum. Let us remember then (what can never be sufficiently inculcated) that God is the author of all events: that none is so small or inconsiderable, as to escape his notice and direction. Every event therefore declares to us the will of God, to which thus declared we should heartily submit. We should renounce our own to embrace it; we should approve and choose what his choice warrants as best for us. Herein should we exercise ourselves continually; this should be our practice all the day long. We should in humility accept the little crosses that are dispensed to us, as those that best suit our weakness. Let us bear these little things, at least for God's sake, and prefer his will to our own in matters of so small importance. And his goodness will accept these mean oblations; for he despiseth not the day of small things. Matt. x, 38.

Whosoever will save his life — At the expense of his conscience: whosoever, in the very highest instance, that of life itself, will not renounce himself, shall be lost eternally. But can any man hope he should be able thus to renounce himself, if he cannot do it in the smallest instances? And whosoever will lose his life shall find it - What he loses on earth he shall find in heaven. Matt. x, 39; Mark viii, 35; Luke ix, 24; xvii, 33; John xii, 25.
For the Son of man shall come — For there is no way to escape the righteous judgment of God.

And as an emblem of this, there are some here who shall live to see the Messiah coming to set up his mediatorial kingdom, with great power and glory, by the increase of his Church, and the destruction of the temple, city, and polity of the Jews.

glossa.text: *From that time,* etc. Behold the reason why the preaching was forbidden, as if he said: Preach me then, when I shall have suffered these things, because before that it does not profit.
*Far be it.* Peter does not wish his own confession to be destroyed, nor does he think that the Son of God can be slain.

*Go.* Above: all those glorious things were promised for the future, not given in the present. *I will build my Church, and to thee I will give the keys,* etc. Which if he had given at once, error would never afterwards have found place in him. *Because thou savourest not.* It does not please thee that I should redeem the world by my death, which is the will of the Father: but thou savourest these things carnally.

*If any man will.* The passion and the resurrection having been foretold to the apostles, he exhorts both them and the crowds to follow. *Let him deny himself.* That which is by oldness, that he may take hold of that which is beyond himself. Vices being removed, let virtue follow: let him take up his cross, and follow me. That which was by oldness, he had denied who said: *But I myself live, now not I.* But that which was beyond himself he had begun: *yet Christ liveth in me ((Gal. II))*. *Let him take up his cross.* That is: the cross is taken up either when the body is afflicted through abstinence, or when the mind is afflicted through compassion for one's neighbour. Paul had the cross of abstinence when he said ((II Cor. XI)): *I chastise my body and bring it into subjection.* And the cross of compassion too, when he says: *Who is weak, and I am not weak?*

*For what doth it profit.* The Church has a time of persecution: it has also a time of peace. These times he designates in his precepts. For in the time of persecution the soul must be laid down, and in the time of peace earthly desires must be broken.

*Or what,* etc. Let neither gains, nor fear, nor anything else draw a man back from salvation: because *what exchange shall a man give,* etc. *I will take the chalice of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord ((Psal. CXV))*. Or: a man will be able to give nothing earthly for a soul that is lost.
*For the Son.* Nor let it seem hard to suffer this: *Because the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, that shall be revealed in us ((Rom. VIII))*.

*There are some.* Because the apostles were untaught, there is promised them even in the present life some consolation, that they may believe the more surely concerning the life to come. *In the kingdom.* In the kingdom of eternal blessedness, or by showing his power in the Church that now is.

echoes.text: Vengeance is mine, and recompense, at the time when their foot slides; for the day of their calamity is at hand. Their doom rushes at them.”
echoes.note: 12:19 cites with the formula 'it is written': 'Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.' The wording reflects the Song of Moses (with a form closer to the Targum/Hebrew than LXX), making divine retribution the ground for renouncing personal revenge.

echoes.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.
echoes.note: 12:20 quotes nearly verbatim: 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so you will heap coals of fire on his head.' Paul takes over the LXX wisdom saying whole as the positive counterpart to renounced vengeance.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge... you shall love your neighbor' is the holiness-code substratum of the whole love-section: 'let love be without hypocrisy,' 'do not avenge yourselves,' and the love of brothers all draw on this command Paul elsewhere makes the summary of the law (13:9).

echoes.text: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”
echoes.note: 'Abhor that which is evil; cling to that which is good' (12:9) closely renders the prophetic imperative 'Hate evil and love good'; the antithetical evil/good pairing matches Amos's covenant ethics.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Do not be wise in your own conceits' (12:16) reproduces 'Be not wise in your own eyes' (LXX), the same proverb that grounded 12:3; here it caps the call to humble association with the lowly.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD and he will save you' is the wisdom source for 'Repay no one evil for evil' (12:17) joined to leaving wrath to God (12:19) — the Proverb already links non-retaliation with reliance on divine vindication.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: 'Depart from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it' underlies both 'abhor evil... cling to good' (12:9) and 'be at peace with all men' (12:18); the twin evil-shunning and peace-pursuing maxims are reflected together.

echoes.text: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
echoes.note: 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes' reinforces the prophetic condemnation of self-conceit that Paul forbids in 12:16.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done' directly parallels the prohibition of returning evil for evil in 12:17.

echoes.text: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
echoes.note: 'Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men' (12:17) echoes 'find favor and good repute in the sight of God and man' (LXX Prov 3:4), the wisdom ideal of conduct visibly good before others.

echoes.text: Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn.
echoes.note: 'Do not fail those who weep, but mourn with those who mourn' is a strikingly close Second Temple parallel to 'weep with those who weep' (12:15); a wisdom maxim of empathetic solidarity rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you God to whom vengeance belongs, you God to whom vengeance belongs, shine out.
echoes.note: 'O LORD, God of vengeance' confirms that retribution belongs to God alone — the theological premise of 12:19 that Paul anchors in Deuteronomy 32:35; possible secondary resonance.

echoes.text: You who love Yahweh, hate evil. He preserves the souls of his saints. He delivers them out of the hand of the wicked.
echoes.note: 'You who love the LORD, hate evil' offers a further scriptural pairing of love and abhorrence of evil behind 12:9.

echoes.text: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
echoes.note: 'God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble' undergirds 'associate with the humble; do not be high-minded' (12:16); the humility motif is the same wisdom orientation James and 1 Peter also draw from this verse.
echoes.lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

echoes.text: Didn’t I weep for him who was in trouble? Wasn’t my soul grieved for the needy?
echoes.note: 'Did I not weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the poor?' anticipates the compassionate mourning-with-the-mourner of 12:15.

echoes.text: But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth. I afflicted my soul with fasting. My prayer returned into my own bosom. I behaved myself as though it had been my friend or my brother. I bowed down mourning, as one who mourns his mother.
echoes.note: The psalmist's mourning and prayer for his persecutors ('I afflicted myself... I went about as one who laments for his mother') parallels both 'weep with those who weep' (12:15) and 'bless those who persecute you' (12:14).

echoes.text: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: The command to love the resident alien 'as yourself' grounds the welcome of strangers behind 'given to hospitality' (12:13) within the same holiness-code love ethic that governs the pericope.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: Abraham's hospitality to the three visitors is the paradigm narrative of welcome that informs the early-Christian virtue 'given to hospitality' (12:13).

echoes.text: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord. For great is the potency of the Lord, And he is glorified of those who are lowly.
echoes.note: 'The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself... what is committed to you, attend to in humility' parallels 'do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble' (12:16) as Second Temple humility instruction.

echoes.text: May Yahweh judge between me and you, and may Yahweh avenge me of you; but my hand shall not be on you.
echoes.note: David's refusal to harm Saul — 'May the LORD avenge me on you, but my hand shall not be against you' — is a narrative enactment of leaving vengeance to God and not repaying evil for evil (12:17, 19).

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
echoes.note: Jesus 'must... suffer many things... and be killed' draws on the Suffering Servant who was despised, rejected, and stricken; the divine necessity ('must') of the Messiah's suffering reflects Matthew's Servant Christology.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'The third day be raised up' echoes 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him,' the OT text most plausibly underlying the recurrent 'third day' resurrection formula.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: 'Get behind me, Satan!' as a rebuke of the adversary echoes 'The LORD rebuke you, O Satan' — Peter unwittingly plays the satan/accuser opposing God's purpose. Thematic and verbal resonance with the rebuke-of-Satan formula.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: The figure of 'the satan' as the adversary who would divert God's servant from his path stands behind naming Peter 'Satan' for setting his mind on human things. Faint, conceptual.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: 'He will render to everyone according to his deeds' closely cites 'to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love, for you render to a man according to his work.' Near-verbatim formula of eschatological recompense; the clearest source-citation in the chapter.

echoes.text: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?
echoes.note: Parallel near-verbatim source for 'render to everyone according to his deeds': 'will he not repay each according to his work?' Matthew's wording fuses the Psalms and Proverbs recompense formula. Together with Psalm 62:12 this is a high-confidence citation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels... coming in his Kingdom' draws directly on the 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to whom dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom are given. Strong verbal ('Son of Man,' 'coming,' 'kingdom,' 'glory') and conceptual borrowing.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.
echoes.note: 'What will a man give in exchange for his life?' echoes 'no man can ransom his brother or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly.' The futility of buying back one's soul with wealth is the shared logic, sharpened by 'gains the whole world but forfeits his life.'

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'With his angels' / 'in the glory of his Father' resonates with 'the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him,' a theophany of the divine coming with the heavenly host that informs the parousia imagery.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' is a further OT recompense text reinforcing the Psalm 62 / Proverbs 24 citation of judgment according to works.

echoes.text: Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.
echoes.note: 'Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life' resonates with the rhetorical 'what will a man give in exchange for his life?' — the supreme value placed on life. Faint, possibly coincidental proverbial overlap.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical 'he will repay to man according to his deeds' continues the Second Temple development of the recompense formula behind 16:27, attesting the currency of the idea in Jesus' milieu.

echoes.text: The soul who sins, he shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.
echoes.note: Individual accountability — each judged for his own conduct, 'the soul who sins shall die' — undergirds the 'render to everyone according to his deeds' principle. Faint, conceptual.

notes.text: Thou knowest — My sincerity, or my sufferings. Visit me - With thy love.
Thy words — The words which from time to time thou didst reveal to me, were by me greedily digested. I am called - I became a prophet by thy authority, therefore, do thou own and defend me.

I sat not — God had all along filled his mouth with such dreadful messages, that his whole prophetical life had been to him a time of mourning and solitude, a time when he sat alone, mourning and weeping in secret for the wrath of God revealed to him against his people.
Why — Jeremiah, though a great prophet, was (as Elijah) a man subject to like passions with other men.

If thou — These are God's words to the prophet, rebuking his distrust in God, and promising him, that if he did return from his distrust in God's providence, he would restore him to the former favour he had with him, and he should be his prophet to reveal his mind to the people; and that if he would separate the precious truths of God from the vile conceits of men, then God would continue him as his prophet, to speak in his name to the people. But - He charges the prophet to keep his ground, and not to go over to wicked men.

The wicked — The wicked Jews. The terrible - And the power of the terrible Chaldeans. The prophet is commanded to abstain from marriage, from mourning, or festival assemblies; hereby representing to them their approaching misery, ver. 1-9. Their sins which caused it, ver. 10-13. Their strange deliverance from Babylon, ver. 14, 15. After that their iniquity is recompensed, ver. 16-18. The prophet's comfort in the calling of the Gentiles, ver. 19-21

glossa.text: *Take me not away in thy patience.* The voice of Christ. As if to say: Thou hast always been long-suffering toward this offending people, but because it has raised up its rashness against me also, be long-suffering no longer. But if thou consider the times of the Lord's passion and of the ruin of Jerusalem, thou wilt see that he was altogether patient. From the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar to the overthrow of the temple forty-two years are reckoned. Because a space of repentance had to be given on account of those who were to believe through the apostles.

*I sat not,* etc. ((HIER.)) The Hebrews judge that these things are spoken in the person of Jerusalem, in that she sat alone, filled with bitterness, etc., *as far as* which will show by the deed that all bitterness was after the likeness of flowing waters.

 *From the face of thy hand. ((ORIG.))* The face of the hand of God is the very stroke of his just judgment, which the man that is proud, etc., *as far as* and if we do not cease from sinning, he adds yet further eternal punishments.

*I sat alone. ((GREG., Moral., lib. IV, c. 35.))* As if to say: While I consider what I now suffer, through the trial of judgment, from the tumult of temporal desires, trembling I seek the retirement of the mind, because still more keenly do I dread those eternal punishments which thou threatenest.

*If thou separate,* etc. ((ID., Moral., lib. XVIII, c. 23.)) For the present world is worthless to God, precious to him is, etc., *as far as* who by speaking what things he can plucks the human soul away from the love of the present age.

*As my mouth. ((HIER.))* Let us consider how great a reward the discourse of a teacher has, if it shall have willed to deliver from error any man, and to call him back from the number of those that sin.

notes.text: Trusted — I have committed my cause and affairs to thee.
For — I dare appeal to thee, because thou knowest I have a deep sense of thy loving-kindness, by which I have been led to love and obey thee.
Sat — Continued with them. I have been so far from an imitation of their wicked courses, that I have avoided their company. Vain - With false and deceitful persons. Go in - Into their company.
Compass — Approach to thine altar with my sacrifices: which I could not do with any comfort, if I were conscious of those crimes, whereof mine enemies accuse me.
House — Thy sanctuary and worship. honour - Thy glorious and gracious presence.

glossa.text:
*A psalm.* ((CASS.)) This psalm admonishes that the fellowships of the wicked be shunned, and that we be joined to the just, because from living together manners are formed.

*Judge.* ((AUG.)) Because after mercy, etc., *as far as* they are carried off by the wind of pride.

 ((CASS.)) *Judge:* it is not the presumption of a just man, but the certainty of God's mercy, which he shews there in hoping in the Lord; then, I shall not be weakened.

*In innocence.* ((AUG.)) Not that of angels, but such as is of men.

*Prove me.* ((CASS.)) That is, first look upon my strength, etc., *as far as* I regard not merits, but the mercy which has made me such.

((CASS.)) *Prove me.* But do thou prove me in temptations, that no sin remain, etc., *as far as* lest any man murmur about them.

*Burn my reins.* ((ID.)) With the fire of thy word, the *heart* with the heat of the spirit. *Heart* for thoughts, *reins* for delights.

*Mercy.* ((CASS.)) Which suffers not that we be tempted above our strength; or that very burning is mercy, not harshness

*I have been well pleased in truth.* ((AUG.)) He to whom his own lie is displeasing, and who himself is pleasing along with her and in her.

*I have not sat.* ((CASS.)) *I have been well pleased* in truth, because I have not sat. *I have hated,* which is to shun evils. *And I will wash,* which is to do right things.

*The vain.* ((CASS.)) *The vain* are they who labour about perishable things; the wicked are heretics, who pervert the Scriptures: those seek superfluous things, these poisonous.
*Of the malignant.* ((ID.)) Who do evils to their neighbours.

*I will wash.* ((AUG.)) By doing penance. *And the altar,* I will adorn my mind with virtues, or faith, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the catholic Church.

 *Among the innocent.* ((AUG.)) Conversing; *that I may hear* from them, that is, that I may learn with what voice thou art to be praised; or, *that I may hear:* Come, ye blessed of my Father.
*The voice of praise* of the Holy Ghost, who teaches to praise thee.

*Lord.* ((CASS.)) He asks that he be not mingled with the wicked in the judgment, because it is not with them, but with the house of God, that he agrees.

*I have loved the beauty.* ((CASS.)) These things therefore will I do, because I have loved to make for thee a comely house, and a place wherein thou mayest dwell in glory, that I may take in something of the glory and the essence of God.

notes.text: Having spoken of faith and its fruit, ver. 3, &c., he comes now to love. The ninth, tenth, and eleventh verses refer to chapter the seventh; the twelfth verse to chapter the eighth; the thirteenth verse, of communicating to the saints, whether Jews or gentiles, to chapter the ninth, &c. Part of the sixteenth verse is repeated from chap. xi, 25. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good — Both inwardly and outwardly, whatever ill-will or danger may follow.
In honour preferring one another — Which you will do, if you habitually consider what is good in others, and what is evil in yourselves.
Whatsoever ye do, do it with your might. In every business diligently and fervently serving the Lord — Doing all to God, not to man.

Rejoicing in hope — Of perfect holiness and everlasting happiness. Hitherto of faith and love; now of hope also, see the fifth and eighth chapters; afterwards of duties toward others; saints, ver. 13 persecutors, ver. 14 friends, strangers, enemies, ver. 15, &c.

Communicate to the necessities of the saints — Relieve all Christians that are in want. It is remarkable, that the apostle, treating expressly of the duties flowing from the communion of saints, yet never says one word about the dead. Pursue hospitality - Not only embracing those that offer, but seeking opportunities to exercise it.
Curse not — No, not in your heart.
Rejoice — The direct opposite to weeping is laughter; but this does not so well suit a Christian.
Mind not high things — Desire not riches, honour, or the company of the great.
Provide — Think beforehand; contrive to give as little offense as may be to any.

Dearly beloved — So he softens the rugged spirit. Revenge not yourselves, but leave that to God. Perhaps it might more properly be rendered, leave room for wrath; that is, the wrath of God, to whom vengeance properly belongs. Deut. xxxii, 35

Feed him — With your own hand: if it be needful, even put bread into his mouth. Heap coals of fire upon his head - That part which is most sensible. "So artists melt the sullen ore of lead, By heaping coals of fire upon its head; In the kind warmth the metal learns to glow, And pure from dross the silver runs below." Prov. xxv, 21, &c.
And if you see no present fruit, yet persevere. Be not overcome with evil — As all are who avenge themselves. But overcome evil with good. Conquer your enemies by kindness and patience.

glossa.text:
*Not slothful.* Cursed is he that does the work of God negligently; the slothful man is without hope in the divine converse. And therefore, that the cold of sloth may be driven off, *Be ye fervent,* etc.

*Fervent in spirit. ((THEOD.))* He called grace the Spirit, etc., *as far as* for this he said. *Instant in prayer.* That is, doing this assiduously.

*Serving the Lord,* etc. As if he should say: Although I have said that ye should be fervent in spirit, yet do not thrust in the words of God everywhere and unseasonably, but be fervent with the opportunity of the time, so that ye may speak the words of faith in fit places, to fit persons, and at a fit time. *Fervent.* The Spirit is fire, with which charity is fervent, whence the Lord says: *I am come to send fire on the earth, and what will I, but that it burn? ((Luc. XII.))*
*Rejoicing in hope.* Being certain of things to come they rejoice, and therefore are patient in tribulation.

*Consenting.* Which is not done with the mouth only, because then is there true humility, if it is not in the tongue alone, lest, presuming upon themselves, they should not suffer with others, but reproach them.

*Give place.* He does not command that the saints should be unwilling to be avenged by God, which the saints cry out for in the Apocalypse, not indeed for the glutting of hatred, but because it is written: *The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge.* But he commands that they, not avenging themselves, give place to the wrath of God, who says: *Revenge to me, and I will repay.* If therefore a good man wills that God punish his enemy, this is not to render evil for evil. Since therefore both the just man and the evil man wish to be avenged by God on their enemies, wherein are they distinguished? The good man desires rather that his enemy be corrected than punished, and when God punishes he is not delighted at his enemy's pain, but that pleases him which pleases the Lord also, because he loves him, and it is God whom he follows in this: *Who raineth upon the just and the unjust ((Prov. XXV))*; and yet even in this world he more sharply reproves the obstinate and at the end will damn them, to whom accordingly vengeance is to be reserved. He gives place to the wrath of his adversary who permits his adversary to do what he will.

*But if he hunger.* Note the strangeness of the conjunction *but.* For it is to be carried on as though neither conjunction had been interposed. Or it can also be read thus, so that neither conjunction is superfluous, as if he should say, not only do ye not defend yourselves, but if, etc.

notes.text: From that time Jesus began to tell his disciples, that he must suffer many things — Perhaps this expression, began, always implied his entering on a set and solemn discourse. Hitherto he had mainly taught them only one point, That he was the Christ. From this time he taught them another, That Christ must through sufferings and death enter into his glory. From the elders - The most honourable and experienced men; the chief priests - Accounted the most religious; and the scribes - The most learned body of men in the nation. Would not one have expected, that these should have been the very first to receive him? But not many wise, not many noble were called. favour thyself - The advice of the world, the flesh, and the devil, to every one of our Lord's followers. Mark viii, 31; Luke ix, 22.

Get thee behind me — Out of my sight. It is not improbable, Peter might step before him, to stop him. Satan - Our Lord is not recorded to have given so sharp a reproof to any other of his apostles on any occasion. He saw it was needful for the pride of Peter's heart, puffed up with the commendation lately given him. Perhaps the term Satan may not barely mean, Thou art my enemy, while thou fanciest thyself most my friend; but also, Thou art acting the very part of Satan, both by endeavouring to hinder the redemption of mankind, and by giving me the most deadly advice that can ever spring from the pit of hell. Thou savourest not - Dost not relish or desire. We may learn from hence,

1. That whosoever says to us in such a case, favour thyself, is acting the part of the devil:

2. That the proper answer to such an adviser is, Get thee behind me:

3. That otherwise he will be an offense to us, an occasion of our stumbling, if not falling:

4. That this advice always proceeds from the not relishing the things of God, but the things of men. Yea, so far is this advice, favour thyself, from being fit for a Christian either to give or take, that if any man will come after Christ, his very first step is to deny, or renounce himself: in the room of his own will, to substitute the will of God, as his one principle of action.

If any man be willing to come after me — None is forced; but if any will be a Christian, it must be on these terms, Let him deny himself, and take up his cross - A rule that can never be too much observed: let him in all things deny his own will, however pleasing, and do the will of God, however painful. Should we not consider all crosses, all things grievous to flesh and blood, as what they really are, as opportunities of embracing God's will at the expense of our own? And consequently as so many steps by which we may advance toward perfection? We should make a swift progress in the spiritual life, if we were faithful in this practice. Crosses are so frequent, that whoever makes advantage of them, will soon be a great gainer. Great crosses are occasions of great improvement: and the little ones, which come daily, and even hourly, make up in number what they want in weight. We may in these daily and hourly crosses make effectual oblations of our will to God; which oblations, so frequently repeated, will soon amount to a great sum. Let us remember then (what can never be sufficiently inculcated) that God is the author of all events: that none is so small or inconsiderable, as to escape his notice and direction. Every event therefore declares to us the will of God, to which thus declared we should heartily submit. We should renounce our own to embrace it; we should approve and choose what his choice warrants as best for us. Herein should we exercise ourselves continually; this should be our practice all the day long. We should in humility accept the little crosses that are dispensed to us, as those that best suit our weakness. Let us bear these little things, at least for God's sake, and prefer his will to our own in matters of so small importance. And his goodness will accept these mean oblations; for he despiseth not the day of small things. Matt. x, 38.

Whosoever will save his life — At the expense of his conscience: whosoever, in the very highest instance, that of life itself, will not renounce himself, shall be lost eternally. But can any man hope he should be able thus to renounce himself, if he cannot do it in the smallest instances? And whosoever will lose his life shall find it - What he loses on earth he shall find in heaven. Matt. x, 39; Mark viii, 35; Luke ix, 24; xvii, 33; John xii, 25.
For the Son of man shall come — For there is no way to escape the righteous judgment of God.

And as an emblem of this, there are some here who shall live to see the Messiah coming to set up his mediatorial kingdom, with great power and glory, by the increase of his Church, and the destruction of the temple, city, and polity of the Jews.

glossa.text: *From that time,* etc. Behold the reason why the preaching was forbidden, as if he said: Preach me then, when I shall have suffered these things, because before that it does not profit.
*Far be it.* Peter does not wish his own confession to be destroyed, nor does he think that the Son of God can be slain.

*Go.* Above: all those glorious things were promised for the future, not given in the present. *I will build my Church, and to thee I will give the keys,* etc. Which if he had given at once, error would never afterwards have found place in him. *Because thou savourest not.* It does not please thee that I should redeem the world by my death, which is the will of the Father: but thou savourest these things carnally.

*If any man will.* The passion and the resurrection having been foretold to the apostles, he exhorts both them and the crowds to follow. *Let him deny himself.* That which is by oldness, that he may take hold of that which is beyond himself. Vices being removed, let virtue follow: let him take up his cross, and follow me. That which was by oldness, he had denied who said: *But I myself live, now not I.* But that which was beyond himself he had begun: *yet Christ liveth in me ((Gal. II))*. *Let him take up his cross.* That is: the cross is taken up either when the body is afflicted through abstinence, or when the mind is afflicted through compassion for one's neighbour. Paul had the cross of abstinence when he said ((II Cor. XI)): *I chastise my body and bring it into subjection.* And the cross of compassion too, when he says: *Who is weak, and I am not weak?*

*For what doth it profit.* The Church has a time of persecution: it has also a time of peace. These times he designates in his precepts. For in the time of persecution the soul must be laid down, and in the time of peace earthly desires must be broken.

*Or what,* etc. Let neither gains, nor fear, nor anything else draw a man back from salvation: because *what exchange shall a man give,* etc. *I will take the chalice of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord ((Psal. CXV))*. Or: a man will be able to give nothing earthly for a soul that is lost.
*For the Son.* Nor let it seem hard to suffer this: *Because the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, that shall be revealed in us ((Rom. VIII))*.

*There are some.* Because the apostles were untaught, there is promised them even in the present life some consolation, that they may believe the more surely concerning the life to come. *In the kingdom.* In the kingdom of eternal blessedness, or by showing his power in the Church that now is.

echoes.note: 12:19 cites with the formula 'it is written': 'Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.' The wording reflects the Song of Moses (with a form closer to the Targum/Hebrew than LXX), making divine retribution the ground for renouncing personal revenge.

echoes.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.
echoes.note: 12:20 quotes nearly verbatim: 'If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so you will heap coals of fire on his head.' Paul takes over the LXX wisdom saying whole as the positive counterpart to renounced vengeance.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge... you shall love your neighbor' is the holiness-code substratum of the whole love-section: 'let love be without hypocrisy,' 'do not avenge yourselves,' and the love of brothers all draw on this command Paul elsewhere makes the summary of the law (13:9).

echoes.text: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”
echoes.note: 'Abhor that which is evil; cling to that which is good' (12:9) closely renders the prophetic imperative 'Hate evil and love good'; the antithetical evil/good pairing matches Amos's covenant ethics.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Do not be wise in your own conceits' (12:16) reproduces 'Be not wise in your own eyes' (LXX), the same proverb that grounded 12:3; here it caps the call to humble association with the lowly.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for Yahweh, and he will save you.
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD and he will save you' is the wisdom source for 'Repay no one evil for evil' (12:17) joined to leaving wrath to God (12:19) — the Proverb already links non-retaliation with reliance on divine vindication.

echoes.text: Depart from evil, and do good. seek peace, and pursue it.
echoes.note: 'Depart from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it' underlies both 'abhor evil... cling to good' (12:9) and 'be at peace with all men' (12:18); the twin evil-shunning and peace-pursuing maxims are reflected together.

echoes.text: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
echoes.note: 'Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes' reinforces the prophetic condemnation of self-conceit that Paul forbids in 12:16.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done' directly parallels the prohibition of returning evil for evil in 12:17.

echoes.text: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.
echoes.note: 'Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men' (12:17) echoes 'find favor and good repute in the sight of God and man' (LXX Prov 3:4), the wisdom ideal of conduct visibly good before others.

echoes.text: Be not lacking to those who weep; And mourn with those who mourn.
echoes.note: 'Do not fail those who weep, but mourn with those who mourn' is a strikingly close Second Temple parallel to 'weep with those who weep' (12:15); a wisdom maxim of empathetic solidarity rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you God to whom vengeance belongs, you God to whom vengeance belongs, shine out.
echoes.note: 'O LORD, God of vengeance' confirms that retribution belongs to God alone — the theological premise of 12:19 that Paul anchors in Deuteronomy 32:35; possible secondary resonance.

echoes.text: You who love Yahweh, hate evil. He preserves the souls of his saints. He delivers them out of the hand of the wicked.
echoes.note: 'You who love the LORD, hate evil' offers a further scriptural pairing of love and abhorrence of evil behind 12:9.

echoes.text: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
echoes.note: 'God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble' undergirds 'associate with the humble; do not be high-minded' (12:16); the humility motif is the same wisdom orientation James and 1 Peter also draw from this verse.
echoes.lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

echoes.text: Didn’t I weep for him who was in trouble? Wasn’t my soul grieved for the needy?
echoes.note: 'Did I not weep for him whose day was hard? Was not my soul grieved for the poor?' anticipates the compassionate mourning-with-the-mourner of 12:15.

echoes.text: But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth. I afflicted my soul with fasting. My prayer returned into my own bosom. I behaved myself as though it had been my friend or my brother. I bowed down mourning, as one who mourns his mother.
echoes.note: The psalmist's mourning and prayer for his persecutors ('I afflicted myself... I went about as one who laments for his mother') parallels both 'weep with those who weep' (12:15) and 'bless those who persecute you' (12:14).

echoes.text: The stranger who lives as a foreigner with you shall be to you as the native-born among you, and you shall love him as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am Yahweh your God.
echoes.note: The command to love the resident alien 'as yourself' grounds the welcome of strangers behind 'given to hospitality' (12:13) within the same holiness-code love ethic that governs the pericope.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood opposite him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth, and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. I will […]
echoes.note: Abraham's hospitality to the three visitors is the paradigm narrative of welcome that informs the early-Christian virtue 'given to hospitality' (12:13).

echoes.text: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, And you will find favor before the Lord. For great is the potency of the Lord, And he is glorified of those who are lowly.
echoes.note: 'The greater you are, the more you must humble yourself... what is committed to you, attend to in humility' parallels 'do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble' (12:16) as Second Temple humility instruction.

echoes.text: May Yahweh judge between me and you, and may Yahweh avenge me of you; but my hand shall not be on you.
echoes.note: David's refusal to harm Saul — 'May the LORD avenge me on you, but my hand shall not be against you' — is a narrative enactment of leaving vengeance to God and not repaying evil for evil (12:17, 19).

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
echoes.note: Jesus 'must... suffer many things... and be killed' draws on the Suffering Servant who was despised, rejected, and stricken; the divine necessity ('must') of the Messiah's suffering reflects Matthew's Servant Christology.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'The third day be raised up' echoes 'on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him,' the OT text most plausibly underlying the recurrent 'third day' resurrection formula.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: 'Get behind me, Satan!' as a rebuke of the adversary echoes 'The LORD rebuke you, O Satan' — Peter unwittingly plays the satan/accuser opposing God's purpose. Thematic and verbal resonance with the rebuke-of-Satan formula.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: The figure of 'the satan' as the adversary who would divert God's servant from his path stands behind naming Peter 'Satan' for setting his mind on human things. Faint, conceptual.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: 'He will render to everyone according to his deeds' closely cites 'to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love, for you render to a man according to his work.' Near-verbatim formula of eschatological recompense; the clearest source-citation in the chapter.

echoes.text: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?
echoes.note: Parallel near-verbatim source for 'render to everyone according to his deeds': 'will he not repay each according to his work?' Matthew's wording fuses the Psalms and Proverbs recompense formula. Together with Psalm 62:12 this is a high-confidence citation.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels... coming in his Kingdom' draws directly on the 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds to whom dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom are given. Strong verbal ('Son of Man,' 'coming,' 'kingdom,' 'glory') and conceptual borrowing.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.
echoes.note: 'What will a man give in exchange for his life?' echoes 'no man can ransom his brother or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly.' The futility of buying back one's soul with wealth is the shared logic, sharpened by 'gains the whole world but forfeits his life.'

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'With his angels' / 'in the glory of his Father' resonates with 'the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him,' a theophany of the divine coming with the heavenly host that informs the parousia imagery.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds' is a further OT recompense text reinforcing the Psalm 62 / Proverbs 24 citation of judgment according to works.

echoes.text: Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life.
echoes.note: 'Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life' resonates with the rhetorical 'what will a man give in exchange for his life?' — the supreme value placed on life. Faint, possibly coincidental proverbial overlap.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: The deuterocanonical 'he will repay to man according to his deeds' continues the Second Temple development of the recompense formula behind 16:27, attesting the currency of the idea in Jesus' milieu.

echoes.text: The soul who sins, he shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.
echoes.note: Individual accountability — each judged for his own conduct, 'the soul who sins shall die' — undergirds the 'render to everyone according to his deeds' principle. Faint, conceptual.

lines: See the bush ablaze on the mountainside, the flame leaping and the branches whole, burning and not burning up.
Here we are; this ground is holy.
Moses turned aside to look, and out of the fire a voice called his name and told him to take off his shoes.
Here we are; this ground is holy.
When he asked who was sending him, the answer was the name above all names: I AM WHO I AM.

The same God who would not be consumed calls us to take up the cross and follow, losing our lives to save them.

turn.trap: Becomes generic self-denial moralism ("give something up") detached from the specific refusal it answers — Peter's, and ours, of a suffering Messiah — or a martyr-glorification that skips past how sharp and immediate the correction is.
turn.hinge: Love for Jesus is exactly what makes Peter say the wrong thing — Jerome will not even call it a devil's suggestion, only misdirected affection — yet Jesus names it "Satan" all the same, because a Christ without a cross is a temptation no matter who offers it.

doors.landing: The love that gets it backwards
doors.claim: Peter's rebuke comes from real affection, not malice, and is corrected all the harder for it — the shape of love has to be re-taught, not just the fact of it.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: This error of the Apostle, proceeding from the warmth of his affection, will never seem to me a suggestion of the devil.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Peter had said, 'Be it far from thee, Lord; this shall not be unto thee'; and had been answered, 'Get thee behind me, Satan'; but the Lord was not satisfied with this rebuke alone.

doors.say: Peter said what he said because he loved Jesus — and love was exactly what needed correcting, not condemning.
doors.do: Have them name one way their love for someone has led them to want to spare them a necessary hard road, and sit with the discomfort of letting go.

doors.landing: Deny yourself, not just your stuff
doors.claim: Self-denial is not asceticism about possessions but ceasing to be who you were, in order to become what you are not yet.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: He denies himself whosoever is changed for the better, and begins to be what he was not, and ceases to be what he was.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: We are to follow our Lord by taking up the cross of His passion; and if not in deed, yet in will, bear Him company.

doors.say: Denying yourself isn't giving something up for Lent — it's ceasing to be the person you've been.
doors.do: Ask them to name one way of being — not one habit — that following Jesus requires them to stop being.

doors.landing: No exchange rate for a soul
doors.claim: The arithmetic of self-preservation never balances — nothing in the whole world can be traded back for the life spent saving it wrongly.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: If you should reign over the whole world, you would not be able to buy your soul.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: He gains the world who does not deny himself... and thence suffers the loss of his soul.

doors.say: There is no amount of the world you could buy back your soul with, once you've spent it protecting the wrong thing.
doors.do: Have them name one thing they're currently spending their life to protect, and ask whether it's worth the trade.

semicontinuous.gravity: Moses meets God at a bush that burns without being consumed and is sent, reluctant, toward a suffering people (Exodus 3); Paul's catalog of love in Romans 12 crests in "overcome evil with good"; and Jesus — immediately after being named the Christ — announces he must suffer and die, and is rebuked by the very man who just confessed him. The nerve: the same confession that names Jesus rightly can, in the very next breath, refuse the shape his mission actually takes.

synthesis.convergence: Moses is sent by a God who has "surely seen the affliction of my people" yet sends him toward more suffering, not around it (Exodus 3); Paul's love-ethic peaks in "overcome evil with good," itself a cross-shaped command (Romans 12); and Jesus names the cross the same day Peter names him Christ. Every reading refuses a rescue that bypasses suffering — deliverance always goes through it.
synthesis.claim: You cannot love Jesus rightly and skip the cross — not his, and eventually not your own.
synthesis.here: For people who want Jesus as comfort without cost, don't soften 'take up your cross' — sharpen it the way Jesus did with Peter: the correction is loving precisely because it isn't gentle.

turn.subtract: Three landings — the miscorrected love, the reshaped self-denial, or the impossible exchange. Choose one and let the others go.
